The Kaul household is in a poor state: Wen is working to recover from the injuries she took on the operation abroad, relearning speech and movement, and Hilo has forgiven neither her nor Shae for keeping her work from him. Kekon itself is changing fast. Espenian money, Espenian soldiers and the Espenian appetite for jade are everywhere, the country's independence is increasingly nominal, and ordinary Kekonese are beginning to ask aloud why two families should control the nation's jade. Anden, home from Espenia and wearing jade again, is training as a doctor rather than as a warrior, on the argument that what jade does to the human body is a medical question nobody has taken seriously.

No Peak discovers that the Mountain has been training Green Bones in a discipline the clans do not teach: a way of concealing a jade aura so that even a skilled user of Perception cannot sense the wearer. Assassins who cannot be felt coming change what is possible in the war, and No Peak has to rebuild its assumptions about its own security from the ground up. Both clans push further abroad, into Espenia, Shotar and beyond, while the black market in jade grows, fed by the drugs that let foreigners tolerate it. Hilo finds himself governing something that is now an international business as much as a martial brotherhood, and dislikes it. The children of the family, Lan's son Niko and Hilo and Wen's own son and daughter, are growing up inside all of this with very different temperaments and very different prospects.

Years pass. No Peak's overseas operations mature, and the clan learns to be a multinational business while remaining a clan, with all the awkwardness that implies; the Mountain does the same. Anden qualifies as a physician and works on the medical side of jade, on tolerance, overexposure and the drugs the clans have used for decades without understanding them, and becomes the person the family turns to when jade is what is killing someone. Shae's authority as Weather Man is at its height while her relationship with Hilo stays cold and correct. Ayt Mada, who has no children, begins to face the problem that a clan built entirely around one person will not outlast her. On Kekon, resentment of foreign influence and of the clans themselves keeps growing, and it starts to organize.

The conflict reaches the mines. A strike over pay and conditions in the jade industry becomes a national crisis, because the clans can neither allow the jade supply to stop nor be seen crushing ordinary Kekonese workers. Foreign powers use the disruption for their own ends, and Kekon's dependence on Espenia becomes a live political argument rather than a background fact. Inside the family, the next generation is coming of age. Niko is being trained as an heir he never asked to be; Ru, Hilo and Wen's son, is a stone-eye who will never wear jade and has grown into a sharp, sociable young man determined to matter anyway; Jaya, their daughter, is a natural fighter with no patience for restraint. Hilo has to decide how much of his own world to force on each of them, and gets it wrong in different ways with each.

More time passes, and the war grinds on at a lower temperature with occasional lethal spikes. Ayt Mada, whose clan is built entirely around her and who is running out of time to arrange what follows her, looks within the Ayt family for a successor she can shape. No Peak works with Espenia and against it by turns as Kekonese sovereignty and the foreign military presence become the central issue in national politics. Anti-clan feeling hardens into an organized movement that regards the Green Bones as a criminal aristocracy and is prepared to act on that belief. Niko, who has never wanted the Pillar's seat and has been told all his life that it is his, spends time abroad working and growing up, and gets his first real taste of a life with no clan in it.

Niko refuses the future the family arranged for him. He leaves the clan and leaves Kekon, choosing to live without jade and without the name, which Hilo takes as a personal repudiation and cannot discuss calmly. Ru, unable to be a Green Bone, builds a public identity instead, organizing and speaking for stone-eyes and arguing that a person's worth in Kekon should not depend on jade, a position that makes him visible, admired, and to people who hate the clans a target. He is murdered. The killing devastates the family and hits Hilo and Wen hardest of all, and it turns the anti-clan movement from a political nuisance into a blood matter that No Peak will pursue for as long as it takes.

The hunt for Ru's killer becomes a permanent undertaking for the clan, carried across borders and years. Jaya, grieving and highly capable, becomes the family's most violent instrument, and her willingness to take the war anywhere creates as many problems as it solves. Kekonese politics turn on the foreign bases and on who actually governs the country, and No Peak has to decide whether the Espenian alliance is worth its price. Hilo and Shae, worn down and out of alternatives, repair their relationship enough to run the clan together properly again. Ayt Mada settles her succession on a young relative raised and educated abroad, who gives the Mountain a modern and respectable face, and fractures open inside the clan almost immediately as an heir with ideas of his own begins to resent the woman who made him. No Peak sees a way out that does not require another generation of killing.

The search for Ru's killer ends, and older history surfaces that changes how both families understand the war they inherited. Niko comes back, on his own terms and by his own decision rather than because he was fetched. Hilo, Shae, Anden and the clan's leadership assemble a settlement: pressure applied inside the Mountain, combined with an offer its next generation can accept, on the shared understanding that the war cannot be won outright and that both clans have paid enough for it. The last obstacle is the two people who have been fighting it personally since the beginning, neither of whom can be bought off, outlasted or persuaded to retire.

The clan war ends. With its succession settled in favor of a leader willing to deal, the Mountain comes to terms with No Peak, and Kekon's two great clans stop trying to destroy each other. What is not settled by negotiation is settled between Hilo and Ayt Mada, who face each other directly at the end of a rivalry that has consumed both their families for three generations: Ayt Mada dies, and Hilo does not outlive her. The Pillar's seat passes to Niko, Lan's son, who takes it as his own decision rather than as the inheritance he grew up resenting, with Shae, Wen, Anden and Jaya around him. Kekon closes the saga as a modern country with a place in the world, its jade traded internationally and its clans pushed into legitimacy, and the family at the center of the story ends it much diminished by the people it has lost and still standing. The last passages belong to the survivors and to their dead.

characters.description: Pillar of the No Peak clan since his elder brother Lan was murdered by the Mountain, and formerly its Horn. Charismatic, hot-tempered and physically dangerous, he leads by personal loyalty rather than policy and takes every attack on the clan as an attack on his family. He is married to Wen, a stone-eye, against the expectations of Kekonese society, and he relies on his sister Shae to run the parts of the clan he has no patience for. The stalemate that ended the last round of the clan war has not changed his intention to destroy Ayt Mada eventually.
characters.name: Kaul Hiloshudon

characters.description: The Weather Man of No Peak, running the clan's businesses, finances and political relationships, a job she took reluctantly and now does with authority. Educated abroad in Espenia, she is the member of the family who understands that Kekon's future will be decided by foreign trade, foreign money and foreign armies as much as by street fighting, and she is pushing the clan's interests overseas. Her relationship with Hilo is close and combative; she is one of very few people who can argue with him and be heard.
characters.name: Kaul Shaelinsan

characters.description: Hilo's wife, and a stone-eye, born unable to perceive or wear jade at all, which Kekonese custom regards as a misfortune close to a disgrace. She manages the Kaul household and the clan's social and charitable face, and is far more ambitious on the clan's behalf than her husband realizes. Her condition makes her invisible to a Green Bone's Perception, and she has already used that once to do work the clan could not otherwise have done.
characters.name: Maik Wen

characters.description: The Kauls' half-Espenian adopted cousin, who graduated at the top of his academy class and then renounced jade entirely after killing the Mountain's Horn with Channeling nearly destroyed him. Unable to be what the clan raised him to be and unwilling to explain himself, he is sent out of Kekon to Espenia, to board with a Kekonese immigrant family in Port Massy and study there. He experiences the arrangement as exile and punishment as much as opportunity.
characters.name: Emery Anden

characters.description: The Kaul grandfather, founder of No Peak and one of the heroes of Kekon's war of independence, now very old, very ill and estranged from the grandson who runs his clan. His authority is long spent, but his name still carries enormous weight in Kekon.
characters.name: Kaul Seningtun

characters.description: The Horn of No Peak, promoted by Hilo after he became Pillar, and the elder of the two Maik brothers. Calm, methodical and enormously loyal, he commands the clan's warriors and manages the daily business of an armed organization that is also fighting a cold war. He is Wen's brother.
characters.name: Maik Kehn

characters.description: Hilo's Pillarman, the younger Maik brother, who carries out the killings and errands the clan does not put in writing. Effective, unsentimental and increasingly reliant on the confidence that comes from being the Pillar's personal instrument.
characters.name: Maik Tar

characters.description: Formerly Lan's Pillarman, now Shae's Shadow, the senior aide who supports the Weather Man and manages her office. Conscientious, discreet and steadying, he is one of the few people who sees how much the job costs her, and his regard for her is more than professional.
characters.name: Woon Papidonwa

characters.description: Pillar of the Mountain clan, which she still intends to make the only clan on Kekon. The last round of the war cost her a Horn and much of her momentum without loosening her grip on her own people. Patient, ruthless and strategically far-sighted, she is playing a longer game than her rivals, and her view is that Kekon's jade must be defended from foreign powers by a single unified authority rather than divided between quarrelling families.
characters.name: Ayt Madashi

characters.description: A smuggler from the Uwiwa Islands who has grown rich moving Kekonese jade to buyers who cannot obtain it legally. Sentimental about his family and utterly pragmatic about everything else, he lives on a fortified estate outside Kekon's reach, guarded by hired fighters who wear stolen jade and take drugs to tolerate it, and he is the reason jade keeps leaving the island.
characters.name: Zapunyo

characters.description: A jadeless opportunist from Janloon who has spent years trying and failing to make himself into somebody through stolen jade. Persistent, resentful and entirely without loyalty, he treats every disaster he survives as evidence that the next scheme will work.
characters.name: Bero

characters.description: A university academic whom Shae becomes involved with: mild, thoughtful and entirely outside the world of clan violence. The relationship gives Shae a life away from the clan, which is exactly why it is difficult to sustain and why her brother distrusts it.
characters.name: Maro

characters.description: Kaul Lan's former wife, who left him before his death and has built a life abroad, far from Kekon, jade and the clans. She has no wish to be found by the Kaul family and no reason to trust them.
characters.name: Eyni

characters.description: A small boy living abroad with his mother, and the son Kaul Lan never knew he had. He has been raised outside Kekon with no knowledge of the clan, which makes him, by the reckoning of the Kaul family, the rightful heir of a dead Pillar.
characters.name: Kaul Niko

characters.description: The informal leader of the Kekonese community in Southtrap, the immigrant district of Port Massy in Espenia. A respected elder who settles disputes, protects his neighbors and keeps a small circle of jade-wearing men around him, he holds a position much like a small clan Pillar's, without any authority the Espenian state recognizes and without the protection Kekonese custom would give him at home.
characters.name: Dauk Losunyin

characters.description: Dauk Losun's son, Espenian-born, a law student with an easy confidence in a country his parents still find foreign. He is impatient with the old-country customs his father maintains and drawn to Anden as someone who is both Kekonese in a way he is not and as adrift in Port Massy as he would be in Janloon.
characters.name: Dauk Corujon

recaps.ending: No Peak's operation against the smuggler Zapunyo succeeds: he is killed and the pipeline carrying Kekonese jade to the Mountain's foreign buyers is destroyed, a serious defeat for Ayt Mada's overseas strategy but not the end of her clan. The victory is paid for at home. Wen, who had been working secretly as the clan's intelligence asset because no Green Bone can sense her, is caught in an explosion and survives with lasting injuries that impair her speech and movement. Hilo learns both that his wife nearly died and that she had been operating for months with his sister's knowledge and his own ignorance, and neither relationship recovers by the end of the book. Anden comes home to Kekon, wearing jade again after taking it up to defend the Kekonese community in Port Massy, and leaves behind a life and a partner in Espenia that he has not given up. Lan's son Niko is now being raised in the Kaul house alongside Hilo and Wen's own children, as No Peak's presumed heir. Kekon closes the book bound tightly to Espenia, with foreign soldiers wearing its jade and foreign money in its politics, and with No Peak and the Mountain still at war, on a board that now covers several countries.
recaps.in_short: With the Kaul grandfather dead and Anden exiled to Espenia, the war between No Peak and the Mountain becomes a global one. Espenia, fighting a proxy war abroad, wants Kekonese jade and the drug that lets foreigners use it, and Shae, as Weather Man, trades access for weapons and political cover, while Ayt Mada's Mountain moves jade to Kekon's enemies through Zapunyo, a smuggler in the Uwiwa Islands. In Port Massy, Anden discovers the Kekonese immigrant community and the criminal crews preying on it, takes up jade again to defend it, and becomes involved with Dauk Cory. The Kauls also discover that Lan left a son, Niko, being raised abroad by his mother, and bring the boy back to Kekon. Hilo commits the clan to killing Zapunyo, and the operation succeeds, but the escape goes wrong: Wen, who has been secretly working for the clan with Shae's help, is badly injured in an explosion and permanently impaired. Hilo learns of the deception, the Mountain remains unbeaten, and the clan war continues on an international stage.

recaps.text: Previously, in Jade City: on the island nation of Kekon, bioenergetic jade grants trained Kekonese, called Green Bones, heightened strength, speed, senses and other abilities, and the jade trade is controlled by clans. In the capital, Janloon, the Kaul family's No Peak clan went to war with Ayt Mada's Mountain clan after she demanded that No Peak submit to a single unified clan under her leadership and Kaul Lan, No Peak's Pillar, refused. During the war Lan's sister Shae, newly home from Espenia, exposed the clan's own Weather Man, Yun Dorupon, as a traitor, and Lan removed him. Lan, secretly weakened by a sabotaged supply of the jade drug shine, was then ambushed and killed by Gont Asch, the Horn of the Mountain. Lan's younger brother Hilo became Pillar, made Shae his Weather Man, installed the Maik brothers Kehn and Tar as Horn and Pillarman, and had the disgraced Yun Dorupon executed against their grandfather's wishes, permanently estranging the two men. A No Peak offensive on New Year's Eve failed to kill Ayt Mada, but the Kauls' adopted cousin Anden killed Gont Asch with a lethal use of Channeling, an act that damaged him so badly he renounced jade for good. The war ended in exhaustion rather than victory, with both clans intact, Kekon's jade drawing serious foreign interest, and Hilo married to Wen, a stone-eye, over his family's objections.

Kaul Sen, the founder of No Peak and a hero of Kekon's war of independence, dies, and Janloon turns out for a funeral that is also a demonstration of the clan's strength. His death removes the last check on Hilo's authority and the last living link to the friendship between the two clans' founders. Anden, who still refuses to wear jade, is sent out of the country: Hilo places him with a Kekonese family in Port Massy, in Espenia, to study, and everyone involved understands the arrangement as exile. The clan war, meanwhile, has cooled into something colder and much larger. Espenia is fighting a war abroad against forces backed by Ygutan, and it wants Kekonese jade and shine for its own soldiers. Both No Peak and the Mountain can see that Kekon's future will be settled by foreign trade and foreign politics as much as by street fighting, and Shae begins pushing the clan's business overseas.

Anden's life in Port Massy is a hard demotion. He is a charity case in a stranger's household, in a country where Kekonese immigrants are treated as second class, and without jade he is nobody in either culture. He begins to learn how the diaspora works: its own informal leadership, its own protection arrangements, and the Espenian criminal crews who have discovered that Kekonese jade is worth a fortune to men willing to take the drug that makes it usable. He meets Dauk Cory, the confident, Espenian-raised son of the community's leading family. In Kekon, Shae negotiates with Espenian commercial and government interests, trading access to jade for advantage, while the Mountain pursues its own foreign strategy: Ayt Mada is moving jade off the island through Zapunyo, a smuggler based in the Uwiwa Islands whose private guards wear stolen Kekonese jade and who sells to whoever pays, including Kekon's enemies.

In Port Massy, Anden is drawn further into the affairs of the Kekonese community of Southtrap, whose respected elder Dauk Losun keeps order among his own people much as a small clan would, without jade laws, without status and without any authority the Espenian state recognizes. The crews' appetite for jade puts that community under mounting pressure. In Janloon, Shae becomes involved with Maro, an academic entirely outside clan life, and finds that a private life and the Weather Man's job do not sit comfortably together, while the clan's leadership argues over how far No Peak should go in binding itself to Espenian interests.

The clans fight through institutions as much as in the streets. Control of the body that governs the mining and distribution of Kekon's jade, and influence over the Royal Council, determine who profits from foreign demand, and both clans buy politicians, businesses and newspapers accordingly. There are killings, formal grievances and duels, and No Peak's overseas ventures are attacked as fast as they are built. Hilo builds a family life alongside the war, as he and Wen raise children and the clan's inner circle closes tighter around him. The Kauls also learn that Lan left a child: his former wife, Eyni, was pregnant when she left him and has been raising the boy, Niko, abroad, with no intention of handing the son of a dead Pillar to the clan she blames for his death. For Hilo the question is not negotiable, because the child is a Kaul and belongs in Kekon with his family. Ayt Mada, still committed to one clan over Kekon, works to make No Peak's foreign strategy fail, betting that Kekon's interests lie with Ygutan and the smuggling network rather than with Espenia, and that the Kauls will be remembered as the family that sold the country's jade to foreigners.

In Espenia, the crews move openly against the Kekonese community, and Anden, who has spent two books insisting he is finished with jade, puts it on again to fight, accepting that he cannot protect anyone as a bystander. He and Cory become close in the process. No Peak also settles the question of Lan's son: Niko is brought back to Kekon and raised in the Kaul house alongside Hilo and Wen's own children, as Lan's heir. On the strategic side, the clan concludes that Zapunyo is the hinge of the Mountain's foreign business and that killing him would cut Ayt Mada off from her buyers. Because he lives outside Kekon, heavily guarded and beyond the reach of any ordinary clan attack, the operation will have to be built slowly, disguised as legitimate business, and carried out with help from outside the clan.

No Peak's alliance with Espenia becomes formal and expensive: Kekonese jade and shine for Espenian soldiers, in exchange for weapons, money and political protection. It also means foreigners wearing jade, trained abroad and relying on drugs rather than a lifetime of discipline, which offends everything Kekonese tradition holds about who jade belongs to and leaves No Peak open to the charge of selling the country. Ayt Mada uses that charge for everything it is worth while running her own trade with Ygutan through the smuggler. Wen, who cannot be perceived by any Green Bone, begins working as an intelligence asset for the clan, going where no Green Bone could go unnoticed. Shae knows, and makes use of it. Hilo does not know, and neither woman intends to tell him.

Preparations for the strike on Zapunyo take over the clan: his compound is studied, his associates are approached, and the operation is concealed inside an ordinary-looking commercial negotiation. Hilo and Ayt Mada meet face to face, each measuring what the other can still afford to spend, and neither offers anything. The costs of the war keep accumulating on both sides in money, in reputation and in dead Green Bones, and Kekon itself is now a country that foreign governments make plans about rather than a place that decides its own affairs. Wen's role in the operation grows, because she can stand next to a jade wearer without being sensed, and Shae lets her take it.

The operation goes ahead in the Uwiwa Islands. Zapunyo is killed, and with him goes the network that carried the Mountain's jade to its foreign buyers. The withdrawal does not go cleanly. An explosion catches Wen, and she survives with serious injuries, including damage that impairs her speech and movement and that will not fully heal. Hilo learns not only that his wife was nearly killed, but that she had been working for the clan for a long time, with his sister's knowledge and with his own kept deliberately in the dark.

The Mountain's foreign pipeline is destroyed and Ayt Mada's strategy is badly set back, but she is not beaten, and No Peak's victory is paid for at home. Wen lives, permanently impaired, and Hilo cannot forgive either her deception or Shae's part in it; the trust between the Pillar and his Weather Man, and between Hilo and his wife, is broken in a way that will not be quickly repaired. Anden comes home to Kekon, wearing jade again and no longer in exile, leaving behind a life and a partner in Espenia that he has not given up. Niko is growing up in the Kaul house as Lan's son and No Peak's presumed heir, alongside Hilo and Wen's own children. Kekon ends the book tied tightly to Espenia, with foreign soldiers wearing its jade and foreign money in its politics, and with both clans still at war on a board that now spans several countries.

characters.description: The second Bennet daughter, intelligent, observant, and quick to form judgments. She is her father's favorite and often meets her mother's agitation with humor.
characters.name: Elizabeth Bennet

characters.description: A wealthy landowner and Mr Bingley's closest friend. At the first local assembly he appears proud, reserved, and dismissive of the company, immediately offending Elizabeth even as the neighborhood takes notice of him.
characters.name: Fitzwilliam Darcy

characters.description: The eldest Bennet sister, admired for her beauty and gentle temper. She is Elizabeth's closest confidante and inclined to see good in nearly everyone.
characters.name: Jane Bennet

characters.description: A rich, friendly young bachelor who rents Netherfield Park. His arrival immediately interests the Bennets and the rest of the neighborhood.
characters.name: Charles Bingley

characters.description: The anxious and talkative mother of five unmarried daughters. She treats the arrival of any eligible wealthy man as an urgent opportunity for the family.
characters.name: Mrs Bennet

characters.description: The dryly humorous master of Longbourn and father of the Bennet sisters. He retreats from family disorder into his library and often answers his wife's agitation with teasing rather than practical help.
characters.name: Mr Bennet

characters.description: The youngest Bennet sister, lively, impulsive, and fascinated by officers. Her parents give her considerable freedom despite her poor judgment.
characters.name: Lydia Bennet

characters.description: Elizabeth's sensible friend and a daughter of Sir William Lucas. Plain, intelligent, and several years older than Elizabeth, she observes the developing attractions in their neighborhood without romantic illusions.
characters.name: Charlotte Lucas

characters.description: Mr Bennet's pompous cousin and the clergyman who will inherit Longbourn. His formal letter announces a wish to repair the strained family connection, and he constantly praises his aristocratic patron.
characters.name: Mr Collins

characters.description: A handsome new militia officer whose easy manners quickly charm Elizabeth and the younger Bennet sisters. His confident sociability contrasts strongly with Darcy's reserve.
characters.name: George Wickham

characters.description: Bingley's fashionable sister, who receives Jane warmly at Netherfield but privately looks down on the Bennet family's social standing and connections.
characters.name: Caroline Bingley

characters.description: Darcy's wealthy and commanding aunt, mistress of Rosings Park and patron of Mr Collins. She expects deference from everyone around her and questions Elizabeth with intrusive certainty.
characters.name: Lady Catherine de Bourgh

characters.description: Mrs Bennet's intelligent, warm-hearted sister-in-law, visiting Longbourn with her family. She offers Elizabeth and Jane steadier, more sympathetic guidance than their parents do.
characters.name: Mrs Gardiner

characters.description: Mrs Bennet's brother, a respectable London tradesman. Calm, generous, and fond of his nieces, he visits Longbourn with his wife and children.
characters.name: Mr Gardiner

characters.description: Darcy's shy younger sister, whom Elizabeth meets at Pemberley. Her affectionate trust in her brother conflicts sharply with Elizabeth's former picture of him.
characters.name: Georgiana Darcy

recaps.ending: Lady Catherine confronts Elizabeth after hearing a rumor that she may marry Darcy, but Elizabeth refuses to promise that she will reject him. Darcy learns of this resistance and gains hope that Elizabeth's feelings have changed. When he and Bingley return to the neighborhood, Bingley proposes to Jane and is accepted. Darcy then tells Elizabeth that his love remains unchanged; she admits that her judgment of him has altered and accepts his proposal. Elizabeth explains herself to the astonished Mr Bennet and persuades him that she truly respects Darcy. Elizabeth and Darcy marry and live at Pemberley, while Jane and Bingley also marry and settle nearby. Lydia and Wickham remain financially careless and frequently seek help. Georgiana grows close to Elizabeth, the Gardiners are warmly welcomed at Pemberley, and even Lady Catherine eventually resumes contact despite her anger at the match.
recaps.in_short: Elizabeth Bennet dislikes the wealthy Mr Darcy after his cold behavior and becomes increasingly prejudiced against him through the charming officer George Wickham. Darcy, meanwhile, falls in love with Elizabeth despite his objections to her family. His first proposal fails because he speaks arrogantly and Elizabeth blames him for separating Jane Bennet from Charles Bingley and for mistreating Wickham. Darcy's explanatory letter forces her to reconsider both men. Their warmer meeting at Pemberley is interrupted when Lydia Bennet runs away with Wickham, threatening the whole family. Darcy secretly finds the pair and pays the costs that make their marriage possible. Once Elizabeth learns what he did, her respect becomes love. Bingley returns and marries Jane. After Elizabeth withstands Lady Catherine's attempt to prevent a match, Darcy proposes again and she accepts. Elizabeth and Darcy marry with a clearer understanding of themselves and each other.

recaps.text: Mr Bingley rents Netherfield Park, exciting Mrs Bennet because she hopes he will marry one of her five daughters. At a local assembly Bingley is friendly and devotes himself to Jane, while his richer friend Darcy refuses to dance with Elizabeth and appears proud. Elizabeth treats the insult lightly but forms a strong dislike of him. Jane is invited to Netherfield, becomes ill after riding there in the rain, and stays with Bingley's sisters. Elizabeth walks to nurse her, giving Darcy an opportunity to observe her intelligence and confidence. His interest grows, though Caroline Bingley mocks Elizabeth and her family. Jane and Elizabeth return to Longbourn with the attraction between Jane and Bingley promising well.

The Bennet household receives Mr Collins, the cousin who will inherit Longbourn. Determined to marry a Bennet daughter, he transfers his attention from Jane to Elizabeth. The sisters also meet the handsome officer George Wickham. Wickham tells Elizabeth that Darcy denied him the church career intended for him by Darcy's father, confirming her bad opinion of Darcy. At the Netherfield ball, Elizabeth endures an awkward dance with Darcy, embarrassing behavior from her family, and Mr Collins's attentions. Jane and Bingley still appear deeply attached, but social differences and the conduct of Jane's relatives trouble Darcy and Bingley's sisters.

Mr Collins proposes to Elizabeth and cannot initially believe her refusal. Mrs Bennet is furious, but Mr Bennet supports his daughter. Collins soon proposes to Charlotte Lucas, who accepts because the marriage offers security; Elizabeth is dismayed by her friend's choice. Bingley and his party abruptly leave Netherfield for London, and Caroline writes as if he will not return. Jane tries to hide her pain. Elizabeth suspects Bingley's friends have deliberately separated the couple. During a London visit Jane receives little warmth from Caroline, strengthening that suspicion. Elizabeth later accepts Charlotte's invitation to visit her new home beside Rosings Park, where Mr Collins serves Lady Catherine de Bourgh.

At Hunsford, Elizabeth meets the overbearing Lady Catherine and again encounters Darcy, who is visiting Rosings. His frequent calls puzzle her. Colonel Fitzwilliam lets slip that Darcy recently saved a friend from an unsuitable marriage, and Elizabeth realizes that he helped separate Bingley from Jane. Darcy unexpectedly proposes, declaring love while emphasizing the inferiority of Elizabeth's connections. Angry at his manner, his interference with Jane, and Wickham's story, she refuses him. The next day Darcy gives her a letter. He explains that Jane seemed indifferent and that Wickham squandered his inheritance, then attempted to elope with Darcy's young sister for her fortune. Elizabeth recognizes weaknesses in her own judgment and begins to reassess both Darcy and herself.

Elizabeth returns home and tells Jane enough of Darcy's letter to correct their view of Wickham. She later travels with the Gardiners to Derbyshire. Believing Darcy absent, they tour Pemberley, where his housekeeper describes him as a generous master and brother. Darcy arrives unexpectedly but behaves with striking courtesy, introduces Elizabeth to Georgiana, and welcomes the Gardiners. Elizabeth's feelings soften as she sees him in his own surroundings. The visit ends when Jane's letters report that Lydia has run away with Wickham. Since the pair are unmarried and missing, scandal threatens every Bennet sister. Darcy hears the news, and Elizabeth leaves convinced that the disgrace has destroyed any possibility between them.

Mr Bennet and the Gardiners search for Lydia and Wickham. Mr Gardiner eventually reports that the couple have been found and will marry if Wickham's debts and financial demands are settled. The Bennets assume Mr Gardiner has paid heavily to save them. Lydia returns as a heedless bride and accidentally reveals that Darcy attended her wedding. Mrs Gardiner then tells Elizabeth the truth: Darcy located the fugitives, paid Wickham's debts, purchased his commission, and arranged the marriage, insisting on secrecy. Elizabeth understands that he acted largely for her sake. News that Bingley and Darcy have returned to Netherfield raises new hope, though neither gentleman immediately explains his intentions.

Bingley renews his courtship of Jane and proposes; she accepts. Lady Catherine arrives at Longbourn to demand that Elizabeth deny rumors of an engagement to Darcy. Elizabeth refuses to surrender her freedom or promise never to marry him. Her defiance gives Darcy reason to hope, and during a walk he again declares his love. Elizabeth now acknowledges her own love and accepts him. They discuss the misunderstandings, pride, and prejudice that kept them apart, and Darcy explains that Elizabeth's rejection changed his conduct. Mr Bennet gives consent after Elizabeth convinces him of her respect for Darcy. Elizabeth and Darcy marry and make Pemberley their home; Jane and Bingley marry as well, while the Gardiners remain valued members of their family circle.

characters.description: An orphaned girl of ten living at Gateshead Hall, the home of her aunt by marriage, Mrs Reed, who took her in unwillingly after the death of Jane's uncle. Plain, small, and passionate, Jane is treated as an unwanted dependent, bullied by her cousins and blamed for every quarrel. Intelligent and fiercely truthful, she longs for affection and justice and will not meekly accept cruelty.
characters.name: Jane Eyre

characters.description: Jane's aunt by marriage and unwilling guardian, a cold, proud widow who despises the orphaned niece left in her care. She indulges her own three children while treating Jane as an inferior, and punishes her harshly, including shutting her alone in the frightening red-room. She resolves to be rid of Jane by sending her away to school.
characters.name: Mrs Reed

characters.description: Mrs Reed's spoiled, overbearing son, some four years older than Jane, who bullies and strikes her while his mother overlooks his behavior. Greedy and idle, he torments Jane as a matter of course and treats her as beneath the family.
characters.name: John Reed

characters.description: The stern, hypocritical clergyman who manages Lowood, the charity school for girls to which Jane is sent. He preaches privation and humility to the pupils while his own family lives in comfort. On meeting Jane he brands her a liar on Mrs Reed's word, and later humiliates her before the whole school.
characters.name: Mr Brocklehurst

characters.description: An older pupil Jane befriends at Lowood, a thoughtful, patient girl who bears the school's harsh punishments without complaint. Devoutly religious, she counsels Jane to endure injustice with forgiveness and to look beyond this life, and she gives Jane the first true friendship she has ever known.
characters.name: Helen Burns

characters.description: The kind and dignified superintendent of Lowood, respected by pupils and teachers alike. She shows Jane and Helen quiet compassion amid the school's severity, clears Jane of Brocklehurst's charge of lying, and becomes a guiding influence and model for Jane.
characters.name: Miss Temple

characters.description: The elderly, motherly housekeeper who welcomes Jane to Thornfield Hall. Kindly and conventional, she runs the household during the frequent absences of its owner and gives Jane her first friendly reception there, though she knows little of the family's secrets.
characters.name: Mrs Fairfax

characters.description: The lively little French girl who becomes Jane's pupil at Thornfield, a ward placed in Mr Rochester's care. Fond of pretty clothes and of songs learned in Paris, she is affectionate but frivolous, and her connection to Rochester is not explained to Jane at first.
characters.name: Adele Varens

characters.description: The master of Thornfield Hall, a dark, abrupt man of about forty whom Jane first meets when his horse slips on the ice and throws him. Blunt, moody, and given to probing conversation, he is drawn to Jane's candor and composure. He keeps his past and the strange happenings in his house closely guarded.
characters.name: Mr Rochester

characters.description: A beautiful, accomplished, and haughty young society lady who visits Thornfield among Rochester's guests. Wealthy in appearance and openly seeking a husband, she treats Jane and the household staff with disdain, and Rochester appears to be courting her, to Jane's private distress.
characters.name: Blanche Ingram

characters.description: The violent madwoman kept in secret confinement on the upper floor of Thornfield, revealed on Jane's wedding day to be Mr Rochester's living wife. A Creole woman from the West Indies whom Rochester married years earlier, she has sunk into raving insanity and has been the hidden cause of the fires and attacks within the house.
characters.name: Bertha Mason

characters.description: The young clergyman who, with his sisters Diana and Mary, takes in the destitute Jane after she collapses at their door on the moors. Handsome, cold, and rigidly self-controlled, he is consumed by an ambition to serve as a missionary and suppresses his own feelings in the name of duty. He helps Jane find work as a village schoolmistress.
characters.name: St John Rivers

recaps.ending: Jane returns to Thornfield to find it destroyed by fire. Bertha Mason, Rochester's mad wife, set the blaze and died leaping from the roof; Rochester, trying to save her and the servants, was left blind and with the loss of a hand. Freed from his first marriage by Bertha's death and humbled by his injuries, he lives withdrawn at Ferndean. Jane, now independent through her inheritance, seeks him out, and the two are reunited. She marries him freely and as an equal, no longer the dependent governess but a wife with means of her own. Their marriage is happy; Rochester in time regains partial sight in one eye, enough to see the birth of their son. The Rivers sisters, Diana and Mary, make good marriages and stay close to Jane, while St John Rivers goes as a missionary to India, where he serves with unbending devotion and, as the book closes, is dying in the faith he lived for.
recaps.in_short: Orphaned Jane Eyre is raised by a cruel aunt, then sent to the harsh Lowood school, where she loses her friend Helen Burns but grows into a self-possessed young woman. Taking a post as governess at Thornfield Hall, she falls in love with its brooding master, Mr Rochester, and he with her, and he proposes. Their wedding is halted by the revelation that Rochester already has a wife: Bertha Mason, a madwoman secretly imprisoned in the house and the cause of its strange terrors. Refusing to be his mistress, Jane flees penniless and is rescued by the Rivers siblings, who prove to be her cousins; she inherits a fortune from an uncle and shares it with them. Resisting a loveless missionary marriage urged by St John Rivers, she seems to hear Rochester call to her and returns to find Thornfield burned, Bertha dead, and Rochester blinded and maimed. Jane marries him, now his equal, and they find lasting happiness.

recaps.text: Jane Eyre is a plain, spirited orphan of ten, raised grudgingly at Gateshead Hall by her aunt Mrs Reed, who despises her and favors her own three children. Bullied by her cousin John and blamed for defending herself, Jane is locked alone in the red-room, the chamber where her uncle died, and is so terrified that she falls ill. Unable to bear the injustice quietly, she at last confronts her aunt with her resentment. Mrs Reed, eager to be rid of her, arranges for Jane to be sent away to Lowood, a charity school run by the harsh clergyman Mr Brocklehurst, whom she warns that the child is a liar. Jane leaves Gateshead friendless but relieved to escape it.

At Lowood, Jane endures cold, hunger, and Brocklehurst's cruel, hypocritical discipline, but finds her first friends: the gentle, dignified superintendent Miss Temple, and a patient, deeply religious older girl, Helen Burns, who teaches her to meet wrong with forgiveness. When Brocklehurst publicly brands Jane a liar, Miss Temple clears her name. A typhus epidemic then sweeps the overcrowded school and many girls die; Helen, already consumed by illness, dies in Jane's arms. The scandal brings reforms to Lowood. Jane remains there eight years, six as a pupil and two as a teacher, until Miss Temple marries and leaves. Restless for a wider life, Jane advertises and is engaged as a governess.

Jane arrives at Thornfield Hall, warmly received by the kindly housekeeper Mrs Fairfax, and begins teaching a lively little French girl, Adele, the ward of the estate's often-absent master. She meets that master, Mr Rochester, when his horse throws him on an icy lane. Abrupt, dark, and moody, Rochester is intrigued by Jane's honesty and draws her into searching conversations, and Jane finds herself increasingly attached to him. Strange things disturb the house: eerie laughter in the night, and a fire set in Rochester's bed, from which Jane saves him. Suspicion falls on a servant, Grace Poole, yet Rochester keeps her on and will not explain, leaving Jane uneasy about the secrets of Thornfield.

Rochester fills Thornfield with fashionable guests, among them the beautiful, scornful Blanche Ingram, whom he seems to be courting, to Jane's quiet pain. During the visit a stranger, Mr Mason, arrives from the West Indies and is mysteriously wounded in the night by something upstairs; Rochester swears Jane to secrecy as he tends him. Jane is then called back to Gateshead, where the dying Mrs Reed at last confesses that three years earlier she hid a letter from Jane's uncle in Madeira, who wished to make Jane his heir. Mrs Reed dies unreconciled. Jane returns to Thornfield, and Rochester, casting off the pretense with Blanche, declares that he loves Jane and asks her to marry him. Astonished and joyful, she accepts.

As the wedding nears, Jane is troubled by omens, and a strange figure enters her room at night and tears her bridal veil. On the wedding morning the ceremony is stopped: a lawyer and Mr Mason declare that Rochester already has a living wife. Rochester admits it and takes the party up to the hidden upper room, where his wife, Bertha Mason, is kept, a violent madwoman who has been the true cause of the fires and the attack. Rochester explains that he was tricked into marrying her for money in Jamaica before her insanity showed, and begs Jane to live with him abroad regardless. Torn between love and conscience, Jane refuses to become his mistress and, in the night, secretly flees Thornfield with almost nothing.

Jane wanders the moors penniless and starving until she collapses at the door of Moor House and is taken in by the clergyman St John Rivers and his sisters, Diana and Mary, who nurse her back to health. Concealing her past, she takes a post as mistress of a village school. St John, cold and ambitious, is preparing to leave as a missionary. He then discovers Jane's true identity and startling news: her uncle in Madeira has died and left her a fortune of twenty thousand pounds, and the Rivers siblings are in fact her own cousins. Overjoyed to have a family at last, Jane insists on dividing the inheritance equally among the four of them.

St John, admiring Jane's usefulness and self-command, presses her to marry him and go with him to India as a missionary's wife, though he offers duty rather than love. Jane is willing to accompany him as a fellow worker but refuses to marry a man who does not love her, and St John coldly persists until he nearly wears down her resistance. At the moment she is about to yield, Jane seems to hear Rochester's voice calling her name across the distance. Shaken and certain, she breaks free of St John and resolves to discover what has become of Rochester.

Jane returns to find Thornfield a burned ruin. She learns that Bertha set the house ablaze and threw herself from the roof to her death, and that Rochester, trying to save the servants and his wife, was blinded and lost a hand. Now free but broken, he lives in seclusion at Ferndean. Jane goes to him, and the two are reunited; she chooses to stay as his wife, and they marry as equals, she now independent and he humbled and dependent on her. In time Rochester recovers enough sight in one eye to see their first child. The couple live happily; Diana and Mary marry well, and St John goes to India, where he labors devotedly and, Jane learns, is nearing death, content in his faith.

characters.description: An orphan raised without affection in her aunt's household. Plain-spoken, observant, and determined to preserve her self-respect, she survives an unhappy childhood and seeks the education and paid work that will let her direct her own life.
characters.name: Jane Eyre

characters.description: Jane's wealthy aunt, who promised her dying husband to care for Jane but regards the orphan as an unwelcome dependent. She favors her own children and treats Jane's resistance as proof of bad character.
characters.name: Mrs Reed

characters.description: Mrs Reed's spoiled son and Jane's older cousin. He bullies Jane with the confidence that his mother and the servants will punish her if she defends herself.
characters.name: John Reed

characters.description: A servant at Gateshead who sometimes offers Jane kindness and conversation, though she also obeys Mrs Reed and helps enforce the child's punishments.
characters.name: Bessie Lee

characters.description: The clergyman who controls Lowood School. He preaches humility and deprivation to the pupils while exercising harsh authority over them, and accepts Mrs Reed's hostile account of Jane before she arrives.
characters.name: Mr Brocklehurst

characters.description: Jane's thoughtful friend at Lowood. Intelligent, patient, and guided by a deep Christian faith, she responds to cruelty with endurance rather than Jane's instinctive defiance.
characters.name: Helen Burns

characters.description: The humane superintendent of Lowood, respected by the pupils. She recognizes Jane's honesty, helps clear her name after Mr Brocklehurst humiliates her, and becomes an important teacher and example.
characters.name: Miss Temple

characters.description: The housekeeper at Thornfield Hall, who welcomes Jane when she arrives as a governess. Her calm manner and ordinary domestic concerns give Jane an initial sense of security in the unfamiliar house.
characters.name: Mrs Fairfax

characters.description: Jane's lively young French pupil at Thornfield. Fond of clothes, presents, and performance, she is Mr Rochester's ward and the reason Jane has been employed as a governess.
characters.name: Adèle Varens

characters.description: The owner of Thornfield Hall and guardian of Adèle. Abrupt, restless, and accustomed to commanding others, he questions Jane closely and finds her direct answers more interesting than conventional flattery.
characters.name: Edward Rochester

characters.description: A beautiful and accomplished woman from a prominent family who visits Thornfield. She and Rochester appear to be natural social equals, and Jane believes they intend to marry.
characters.name: Blanche Ingram

characters.description: A visitor from the West Indies whose arrival at Thornfield unsettles Rochester. He knows something about Rochester's earlier life and becomes involved in a violent, unexplained incident during his stay.
characters.name: Richard Mason

characters.description: Rochester's wife, kept under supervision in the upper part of Thornfield after years of severe mental illness and violence. Her existence, concealed from Jane, makes Rochester's attempted marriage to Jane unlawful.
characters.name: Bertha Antoinetta Mason

characters.description: A serious young clergyman who shelters Jane after she collapses near his home. Disciplined and ambitious for missionary work, he respects endurance and usefulness but distrusts emotional claims that conflict with duty.
characters.name: St John Rivers

characters.description: St John's warm, educated sister, who receives the destitute Jane into Moor House. She offers Jane companionship founded on shared interests and affection rather than dependence.
characters.name: Diana Rivers

recaps.ending: After rejecting St John Rivers's proposal of a loveless missionary marriage, Jane returns to seek Rochester. Thornfield has burned down; Bertha Mason set the fire and died after jumping from the roof, while Rochester was injured trying to save the household and lost his sight and one hand. Jane finds him living in seclusion at Ferndean. Now financially independent and able to meet him freely, she assures him that she has returned by choice. They marry. Rochester gradually recovers sight in one eye and is able to see their first child. Diana and Mary Rivers also marry, while St John continues his missionary work in India and appears to be approaching death with the same absolute commitment that governed his life. Jane closes as Rochester's partner rather than his employee or dependent, with the legal obstacle removed and the imbalance between them greatly reduced.
recaps.in_short: Orphaned Jane Eyre is abused at Gateshead and sent to the harsh Lowood School, where friendship and education help her become a teacher. Seeking a wider life, she becomes governess at Thornfield Hall and falls in love with its owner, Edward Rochester. Their planned marriage is stopped by the revelation that Rochester already has a living wife, Bertha Mason, confined at Thornfield because of severe mental illness. Jane refuses to become his mistress and flees. Destitute, she is rescued by the Rivers siblings, discovers they are her cousins, and inherits a fortune that she shares with them. St John Rivers asks her to marry him and join his missionary work, but she refuses a union without love. Jane returns to find Thornfield burned, Bertha dead, and Rochester blinded and maimed. Independent and still loving him, Jane reunites with Rochester and marries him; he later regains enough sight to see their child.

recaps.text: Jane Eyre is an orphan living at Gateshead with her aunt, Mrs Reed, and cousins who resent her presence. After John Reed attacks her and Jane resists, she is locked in the room where her uncle died and becomes terrified and ill. Jane finally tells Mrs Reed that her cruelty has destroyed any claim to affection. Mrs Reed sends her to Lowood, a charity school run by the severe clergyman Mr Brocklehurst, having first described Jane to him as deceitful. At Lowood, poor food, cold rooms, and strict discipline replace the comforts of Gateshead, but Jane begins to find companionship and the possibility of education.

At Lowood, Jane befriends Helen Burns, whose patience and faith differ sharply from Jane's anger at injustice. Mr Brocklehurst publicly humiliates Jane as a liar, but Miss Temple hears her story, verifies it, and restores her reputation. Disease spreads through the badly managed school, exposing its neglect and forcing reforms. Helen, already ill with tuberculosis, dies with Jane beside her. Jane remains at the improved school for years, first as a pupil and then as a teacher. When Miss Temple leaves, Jane realizes how narrow her own life has become and advertises for a new post. She is hired as governess to Adèle Varens at Thornfield Hall, where the housekeeper Mrs Fairfax receives her kindly.

Jane begins teaching Adèle and meets Thornfield's owner, Edward Rochester, after encountering him on the road. Rochester is abrupt and searching in conversation but values Jane's honesty. Strange laughter and disturbances in the house are attributed to the servant Grace Poole. One night Jane wakes to find Rochester's bed curtains burning and saves him; he makes her keep the incident private. Jane's attachment to him deepens, although she assumes the difference in wealth and status rules out any future between them. When Rochester hosts a fashionable party, the beautiful Blanche Ingram appears to be his intended bride. Jane watches their apparent courtship and tries to master her jealousy.

A visitor named Richard Mason arrives from the West Indies and is secretly attacked during the night. Jane helps Rochester tend him without being told who caused his wounds. Jane later returns to Gateshead, where the dying Mrs Reed admits that she concealed a letter from Jane's uncle John Eyre, who had wished to adopt her. Back at Thornfield, Rochester leads Jane to believe she must leave because he will marry Blanche, then reveals that he loves Jane and asks her to marry him instead. Jane accepts. Uneasy signs accompany the engagement, including damage to Jane's wedding veil, but Rochester continues to dismiss her fears and presses toward the ceremony.

Jane and Rochester's wedding is interrupted by the declaration that Rochester is already married. His wife, Bertha Mason, is alive and confined at Thornfield under Grace Poole's care; she caused the fire and attacked her brother Richard. Rochester explains the disastrous marriage arranged in his youth and asks Jane to live with him abroad despite the legal barrier. Jane still loves him but refuses to sacrifice her principles or independence, and she leaves secretly. After exhausting her money, she collapses near Moor House and is rescued by the siblings St John, Diana, and Mary Rivers. Jane recovers, takes work as a village schoolteacher, and begins building a modest life apart from Rochester.

St John discovers Jane's identity and tells her that her uncle John Eyre has died, leaving her a large fortune. She also learns that the Rivers siblings are her cousins. Delighted to have family, Jane divides the inheritance equally among the four of them. St John plans missionary work in India and trains Jane to assist him. He asks her to marry him, not from romantic love but because he considers her disciplined enough to be a missionary's wife. Jane offers to go as his colleague but refuses the marriage. Under the force of his will she nearly yields, then seems to hear Rochester calling her name from a great distance. She decides to learn what has happened to him.

Jane returns to Thornfield and finds it a burned ruin. Bertha set the house on fire and died after jumping from the roof; Rochester saved the servants but was blinded and lost a hand. He now lives in isolation at Ferndean. Jane goes to him with independent means and assures him that she has chosen to return. With Bertha dead and Jane no longer economically dependent on Rochester, they marry and establish a companionate life. Rochester later recovers sight in one eye and sees their first child. Diana and Mary Rivers find happy marriages, while St John remains in India, wholly committed to missionary work even as his health fails. Jane's long effort to unite love, conscience, family, and freedom ends with a marriage she can enter as an equal moral agent.

characters.description: An orphan of ten living as an unwanted dependent in her aunt's comfortable home at Gateshead. Thoughtful, observant, and passionate about fairness, Jane has learned to endure isolation but resists when her cousin John bullies her and the household treats her as morally inferior.
characters.name: Jane Eyre

characters.description: Jane's widowed aunt and guardian, who promised her dying husband that she would care for the orphan. She resents Jane, favors her own children, and interprets the girl's resistance to mistreatment as deceit and ingratitude.
characters.name: Mrs Reed

characters.description: Mrs Reed's fourteen-year-old son, indulged by his family and accustomed to commanding Jane. He torments her, throws a book at her, and then has her blamed when she defends herself.
characters.name: John Reed

characters.description: A servant at Gateshead who can be impatient with Jane but also tells her stories, tends her when she is ill, and shows more warmth than the Reed family does. Jane values Bessie's occasional affection even while recognizing her readiness to accept the household's judgments.
characters.name: Bessie Lee

characters.description: The clergyman who controls Lowood Institution, the charity school proposed for Jane. Severe in dress and manner, he praises deprivation as moral training and accepts Mrs Reed's claim that Jane is deceitful before the girl has any chance to establish herself.
characters.name: Mr Brocklehurst

characters.description: The superintendent of Lowood, dignified and compassionate within an institution marked by cold, hunger, and strict discipline. She recognizes the pupils' needs, treats them with respect, and makes a strong impression on the newly arrived Jane.
characters.name: Miss Temple

characters.description: An older Lowood pupil whom Jane sees being punished without protest. Intelligent, reflective, and deeply religious, Helen responds to hardship with patience rather than rebellion and becomes Jane's first close friend.
characters.name: Helen Burns

characters.description: The elderly housekeeper at Thornfield Hall, who welcomes Jane on her arrival as governess. Her friendly, practical manner makes the quiet house feel less forbidding, though Jane initially mistakes her for its owner.
characters.name: Mrs Fairfax

characters.description: A lively French child living at Thornfield as Mr Rochester's ward and placed under Jane's instruction. Fond of dresses, songs, and attention, she speaks freely about her former life with her mother and quickly warms to her new governess.
characters.name: Adèle Varens

characters.description: A servant at Thornfield employed in sewing and other household work. Mrs Fairfax identifies her as the source of a strange, disquieting laugh heard from an upper floor, making her an object of Jane's curiosity.
characters.name: Grace Poole

characters.description: The master of Thornfield, first encountered by Jane on a wintry road after his horse slips. Abrupt, physically unimposing, and accustomed to questioning others closely, he returns to the hall with an injury and is revealed as Jane's employer and Adèle's guardian.
characters.name: Edward Rochester

characters.description: A beautiful, accomplished guest at Thornfield from a socially prominent family. She performs confidently before the house party and appears to be the woman Rochester intends to court, while treating governesses and social inferiors with open disdain.
characters.name: Blanche Ingram

characters.description: A visitor newly arrived from the West Indies who has known Rochester abroad. His unexpected presence disturbs his host, although Mason himself behaves cordially among the Thornfield guests.
characters.name: Richard Mason

characters.description: Rochester's living wife, Bertha Antoinetta Mason, whose existence is disclosed when his wedding to Jane is stopped. Now financially independent and able to meet him freely, she tells him that she has come to stay. They marry, with Adèle placed at a better school and remaining part of Jane's life. Rochester gradually recovers enough sight in one eye to see their first child. Jane reports ten years of an equal and happy marriage. Diana and Mary Rivers also marry, while St John continues his missionary work in India. His health is failing, and the novel closes with his unwavering expectation of death and spiritual reward. Seeking independence, she becomes governess at Thornfield Hall and falls in love with its troubled master, Edward Rochester. Their wedding is stopped by the discovery that Rochester already has a living wife, Bertha Mason, confined at Thornfield because of severe mental illness. Jane refuses to become his mistress and leaves with almost nothing. The Rivers siblings rescue her; she later learns they are her cousins and shares a large inheritance with them. She rejects St John Rivers's proposal that she marry him for missionary work and returns to Rochester. Bertha has burned Thornfield and died, while Rochester was blinded and maimed rescuing others. Jane reunites with him at Ferndean, marries him as an independent equal, and builds the loving home she had long lacked. Rochester eventually regains partial sight.

recaps.text: Ten-year-old Jane Eyre is an orphan living at Gateshead with her aunt, Mrs Reed, and the Reed children. The family treats her as an inferior dependent, and her cousin John bullies her. When Jane fights back after he injures her, she is locked in the red-room where her uncle died. Terror and distress make her ill. The apothecary Mr Lloyd recognizes her misery and suggests school, an escape Jane wants. Mrs Reed arranges to send her to Lowood Institution under the severe clergyman Mr Brocklehurst, telling him that Jane is deceitful. Before leaving, Jane finally tells her aunt how cruelly she has been treated. At Lowood, Jane finds cold rooms, inadequate food, rigid discipline, and rows of girls expected to endure deprivation quietly. The superintendent, Miss Temple, provides one of the few signs of humane authority.

At Lowood, Jane befriends Helen Burns, an intelligent older pupil whose religious patience contrasts with Jane's anger at injustice. Brocklehurst visits and publicly labels Jane a liar, ordering the school to shun her, but Miss Temple listens to Jane's account and clears her name after checking it. A typhus outbreak exposes Lowood's neglect and kills many pupils. Helen, already dying of consumption, spends her final night with Jane and dies beside her. Public scrutiny brings reforms, and conditions improve. Jane remains for eight years, first as a pupil and then as a teacher. When Miss Temple marries and leaves, Jane recognizes her desire for a wider life. She advertises for a governess position and receives an offer from Mrs Fairfax at Thornfield Hall. After a last visit from Bessie, Jane leaves the institution that shaped both her discipline and her hunger for independence.

Jane arrives at Thornfield and becomes governess to Adèle Varens, the lively French ward of the absent master, Edward Rochester. Mrs Fairfax manages the household, while an odd laugh from an upper floor is attributed to servant Grace Poole. Jane meets Rochester without knowing him when his horse falls on the road; after his return he questions her closely and shows interest in her drawings and character. His abrupt manner and troubled history intrigue her, and their conversations begin to break Thornfield's isolation. One night Jane hears the strange laugh, smells smoke, and discovers Rochester asleep with his bed curtains burning. She wakes him and helps extinguish the fire. Rochester again blames Grace Poole but asks Jane to keep the event private. His gratitude and emotion strengthen Jane's attachment, even as his secrecy makes the danger in the house harder to understand.

Rochester hosts a large party at Thornfield, including the beautiful Blanche Ingram, who appears to be his intended bride. Jane tries to suppress her feelings while watching their apparent courtship and enduring Blanche's contempt for governesses. Rochester disguises himself as a fortune-telling woman to question his guests and probe Jane's emotions. The gathering is disrupted by the arrival of Richard Mason from the West Indies, whose presence visibly alarms Rochester. During the night, a cry sounds from the upper floor. Mason has been attacked and badly wounded. Rochester secretly brings Jane to tend him while forbidding the two to speak, then sends Mason away under medical care before morning. Grace Poole is once again presented as responsible, but her continued employment and Rochester's evasions persuade Jane that Thornfield conceals a more complicated danger.

Jane returns to Gateshead after Mrs Reed suffers a stroke. Her aunt remains bitter and reveals that she concealed a letter from Jane's uncle John Eyre, who had wished to adopt her. Mrs Reed dies without reconciliation. Back at Thornfield, Rochester leads Jane to believe he will marry Blanche, then declares his love for Jane and proposes. She accepts, despite Mrs Fairfax's concern about their unequal positions. Ominous events precede the wedding, including the destruction of Jane's veil. At the ceremony, a solicitor and Richard Mason stop the marriage by proving that Rochester already has a living wife. He takes the group to the upper floor, where Bertha Mason is confined under Grace Poole's care; Bertha caused the fire and attacks. Rochester explains the disastrous marriage and asks Jane to live with him abroad despite the legal bond. She loves him but refuses a relationship that would violate her conscience. Before dawn, she leaves Thornfield alone with little money.

Jane's money is lost during her flight, and she wanders hungry across the moors after being refused shelter and work. Near collapse, she is admitted to Moor House by the Rivers siblings: the clergyman St John and his sisters Diana and Mary. Jane withholds her past and uses the name Jane Elliott, but their kindness gives her a temporary home. St John finds her work teaching a small village school for poor girls. The position is humble, yet Jane values the independence and gradually gains the pupils' trust. She meets Rosamond Oliver, the wealthy and charming daughter of the school's benefactor, and sees that she and St John are attracted to each other. St John suppresses the possibility of marriage because he believes Rosamond is unsuited to the difficult missionary life he intends to lead.

St John discovers Jane's real identity while tracing news from a solicitor: her uncle John Eyre has died and left her a fortune of twenty thousand pounds. She also learns that St John, Diana, and Mary are her cousins. Delighted to have relatives more than wealth, Jane divides the inheritance equally among the four of them and restores Moor House as a shared home. St John prepares for missionary work in India and trains Jane to assist him. He asks her to marry him, not from romantic love but because he considers her suitable for the work. Jane offers to accompany him as a cousin, but refuses a loveless marriage that she believes would destroy her. Under the pressure of his will and religious appeal she nearly consents. Then, in a moment she cannot explain, she hears Rochester's voice calling her name from far away. She resolves to discover what has happened to him.

Jane travels back to Thornfield and finds it a burned ruin. She learns that Bertha set the house on fire, climbed to the roof, and died in a fall. Rochester got the servants out but was gravely injured when the building collapsed, losing one hand and his sight. Jane finds him living in seclusion at Ferndean. Her return restores his hope; now independently wealthy and free to choose, she can join him without becoming dependent or compromising her principles. They marry and form a quiet, close partnership. Adèle remains under Jane's care and is moved to a kinder school. Over time Rochester recovers enough sight in one eye to see their first child. Jane looks back after ten years of marriage as content and equal in the relationship. Diana and Mary marry as well, while St John remains in India, devoted to missionary work and approaching death with certainty in his calling.

Heathcliff returns wealthy and takes revenge across two generations, gaining both family estates and forcing Catherine's daughter to marry his sickly son. The elder Catherine's death leaves him obsessed rather than satisfied. The younger Catherine eventually befriends and loves Hareton Earnshaw, whom Heathcliff kept uneducated. Brocklehurst visits Lowood and publicly brands Jane a liar, ordering the school to avoid her. Miss Temple hears Jane's account, verifies it, and restores her standing. A typhus epidemic then spreads through the badly managed institution, revealing the consequences of poor food and unhealthy conditions. Helen Burns is not among the fever cases but is dying of consumption. Jane goes to her room at night, and Helen dies while they are together. Public scrutiny brings changes to Lowood. Jane remains there for eight years, first learning and then teaching. When Miss Temple marries and leaves, Jane recognizes that she wants a wider life. She advertises her services and accepts a governess position at Thornfield Hall.

He asks her to marry him because he considers her suited to the work, not because he loves her. Jane offers a familial partnership but rejects a loveless marriage. Under sustained pressure she nearly yields, then believes she hears Rochester calling her and resolves to find him.

He later discovers that Jane's uncle has died and left her a large fortune, and that Jane and the Rivers siblings are cousins. Jane divides the inheritance with them, gaining both independence and family. St John prepares for missionary work in India and asks Jane to marry him as a useful partner rather than from love. She refuses a marriage without affection. After seeming to hear Rochester calling her from a distance, she returns to Thornfield and finds it burned. Bertha died in the fire; Rochester was blinded and lost a hand while rescuing the household. Jane reunites with him at Ferndean, marries him freely, and later reports that he recovered sight in one eye.

The collection turns to Wuthering Heights. Mr Lockwood, tenant of Thrushcross Grange, makes two difficult visits to his landlord Heathcliff. He encounters Hareton Earnshaw, the widowed Catherine Linton, the servant Joseph, and a household in which nobody explains the relationships. A snowstorm forces him to spend the night. In a disused chamber he finds childhood writing linked to Catherine Earnshaw and dreams that a ghostly child begs to enter through the window. Heathcliff's desperate response to Catherine's name reveals that the past still dominates him. Back at the Grange, Lockwood asks his housekeeper Nelly Dean to explain what he has seen, and she begins the history of the Earnshaw family and the orphan brought home by its former master.

The collection turns to Wuthering Heights. Tenant Lockwood visits his landlord Heathcliff and meets the hostile household of Hareton Earnshaw and Catherine Linton. Forced to stay in a storm, Lockwood sleeps in an old room connected to Catherine Earnshaw and has a terrifying encounter at the window that he interprets as her ghost. His housekeeper Nelly Dean begins the family's history. The old Mr Earnshaw brought the orphan Heathcliff home; Catherine befriended him, but her brother Hindley hated him. After gaining control, Hindley reduced Heathcliff to a laborer. Catherine also became close to the refined Edgar Linton. She accepted Edgar's proposal while telling Nelly that her bond with Heathcliff was deeper, but Heathcliff overheard only her claim that marrying him would lower her and disappeared.

Catherine marries Edgar Linton and settles at Thrushcross Grange. Heathcliff returns after three years, unexpectedly prosperous and controlled in manner, but determined to repay old injuries. He visits Wuthering Heights, where Hindley accepts him as a gambling companion and risks the estate against him. Isabella Linton develops a romantic interest in Heathcliff. Catherine warns that he is not the figure Isabella imagines, while Heathcliff sees the attraction as another way to strike at Edgar. Quarrels divide the household. Catherine shuts herself away, refuses food, and becomes seriously ill. Heathcliff elopes with Isabella and brings her to Wuthering Heights, where she discovers that marriage has placed her within a violent and vindictive household.

Catherine marries Edgar. Heathcliff returns three years later with wealth and polished manners, intending revenge. He encourages Hindley's gambling until Wuthering Heights is mortgaged to him and uses Isabella Linton's infatuation to wound Edgar. Heathcliff elopes with Isabella and treats her cruelly. Conflict with the men contributes to Catherine's severe illness. Nelly allows Heathcliff to visit her in secret; their painful reunion affirms their attachment but resolves nothing. Catherine dies after giving birth to a daughter. Isabella escapes, Hindley dies in Heathcliff's debt, and Heathcliff takes the estate while keeping Hareton dependent and uneducated. Years later Isabella dies, and Heathcliff takes custody of their frail son Linton. He begins arranging contact between Linton and Edgar's sheltered daughter Catherine in order to gain Thrushcross Grange through their marriage.

Young Catherine grows up at Thrushcross Grange under Edgar's protection, largely unaware of Wuthering Heights. After Isabella dies, Edgar brings her sickly son Linton north, but Heathcliff claims him. Catherine encounters Hareton and later begins corresponding with Linton. Heathcliff encourages the connection because marriage would give his son a path to the Grange. Nelly stops the correspondence, yet Catherine secretly visits Linton. He alternates between affection, selfish complaints, and fear of displeasing his father. Edgar's health declines. Although he eventually permits meetings between the cousins, Linton is visibly failing and acts under Heathcliff's pressure. Heathcliff then traps Catherine and Nelly at Wuthering Heights, refusing to release Catherine to her dying father until she marries Linton.

Catherine escapes Wuthering Heights in time to be with Edgar before he dies, but the forced marriage has already placed her inheritance within Heathcliff's reach. Heathcliff brings her back to his house. The ailing Linton soon dies after making his father his heir, so Heathcliff now controls both estates and Catherine has no independent home. Lockwood visits before leaving the district and sees Catherine ridicule Hareton's effort to educate himself. Months later, he returns and learns that Nelly has moved to Wuthering Heights. Catherine has recognized the cruelty of her contempt, apologized to Hareton, and offered to teach him to read. Hareton responds with loyalty, and the two become close despite Heathcliff's efforts to make them enemies.

Young Catherine pities Linton and visits him despite Nelly's objections. Edgar is dying, while Heathcliff pressures his fearful son to secure the marriage. Heathcliff finally imprisons Catherine and Nelly at Wuthering Heights and withholds Catherine from her father until she marries Linton. She escapes in time to see Edgar before his death, but her property passes through her husband. Linton soon dies after naming Heathcliff his heir, leaving Catherine trapped and dispossessed. Lockwood leaves the district after seeing her contempt for the uneducated Hareton. When he returns months later, Nelly explains that Catherine apologized, began teaching Hareton to read, and fell in love with him. Their closeness makes revenge seem empty to Heathcliff. Haunted by Catherine Earnshaw's memory, he stops eating and dies. Catherine and Hareton plan to marry and move to the Grange, uniting the families and estates.

Mrs Fairfax manages the household, while an odd laugh from an upper floor is attributed to servant Grace Poole. Jane meets Rochester without knowing him when his horse falls on the road; after his return he questions her closely and shows interest in her drawings and character. His abrupt manner and troubled history intrigue her, and their conversations begin to break Thornfield's isolation. One night Jane hears the strange laugh, smells smoke, and discovers Rochester asleep with his bed curtains burning. She wakes him and helps extinguish the fire. Rochester again blames Grace Poole but asks Jane to keep the event private. His gratitude and emotion strengthen Jane's attachment, even as his secrecy makes the danger in the house harder to understand.

Rochester hosts a large party at Thornfield, including the beautiful Blanche Ingram, who appears to be his intended bride. Jane tries to suppress her feelings while watching their apparent courtship and enduring Blanche's contempt for governesses. Rochester disguises himself as a fortune-telling woman to question his guests and probe Jane's emotions. The gathering is disrupted by the arrival of Richard Mason from the West Indies, whose presence visibly alarms Rochester. During the night, a cry sounds from the upper floor. Mason has been attacked and badly wounded. Rochester secretly brings Jane to tend him while forbidding the two to speak, then sends Mason away under medical care before morning. Grace Poole is once again presented as responsible, but her continued employment and Rochester's evasions persuade Jane that Thornfield conceals a more complicated danger.

Jane returns to Gateshead after Mrs Reed suffers a stroke. Her aunt remains bitter and reveals that she concealed a letter from Jane's uncle John Eyre, who had wished to adopt her. Mrs Reed dies without reconciliation. Back at Thornfield, Rochester leads Jane to believe he will marry Blanche, then declares his love for Jane and proposes. She accepts, despite Mrs Fairfax's concern about their unequal positions. Ominous events precede the wedding, including the destruction of Jane's veil. At the ceremony, a solicitor and Richard Mason stop the marriage by proving that Rochester already has a living wife. He takes the group to the upper floor, where Bertha Mason is confined under Grace Poole's care; Bertha caused the fire and attacks. Rochester explains the disastrous marriage and asks Jane to live with him abroad despite the legal bond. She loves him but refuses a relationship that would violate her conscience. Before dawn, she leaves Thornfield alone with little money.

Jane's money is lost during her flight, and she wanders hungry across the moors after being refused shelter and work. Near collapse, she is admitted to Moor House by the Rivers siblings: the clergyman St John and his sisters Diana and Mary. Jane withholds her past and uses the name Jane Elliott, but their kindness gives her a temporary home. St John finds her work teaching a small village school for poor girls. The position is humble, yet Jane values the independence and gradually gains the pupils' trust. She meets Rosamond Oliver, the wealthy and charming daughter of the school's benefactor, and sees that she and St John are attracted to each other.
